utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Madam Usher, could I ask you to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before the witness comes into the courtroom, there was a matter that I was going to respond to in relation to the proofing session of November last year and that was in relation to a comment that the witness had made that he had informed the Office of the Prosecutor in relation to a correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: As it turns out, I've had an opportunity to review the notes. There's no record of any such communication taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That leaves two possibilities, either the record is not complete or it has not been corrected. So it's better to have a full -- of course I can't say what it is, neither can Ms. Loukas and I'm afraid neither can you but thank you for the information. Ms. Loukas, you are informed. Whether this is satisfactory or not is another matter or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, there's just one matter I also need to raise very briefly before the witness comes in and that is that our interpreter is not present in court at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed about that. He will come soon but he has to go through all the bureaucracy, is that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, precisely, Your Honour. The situation was as I was coming through the foyer he was there, but as Defence counsel we're not able to bring people into the building; it's only the Prosecution or the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it he will arrive soon. Measures have been taken to bring him into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It is just unfortunate that there is that systemic failure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Djokanovic, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave before your testimony on Monday. Ms. Loukas, first of all, the 60 per cent rule if you look realistically at what happened, doesn't bring you to five hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I mean, I reviewed the transcript, and I realised that mathematics is not my strong suit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think you've received the message that you get a half an hour after the first break.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I have received the message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, when you were giving evidence on Tuesday, you gave evidence in relation to -- that's at page 29 of the transcript on the 15th of March for the benefit of the Court and counsel. You were saying that at that point in time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have the paginated version not the LiveNote version so if I could just do a reconciliation of that to see when each of the sessions commences on the final version.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the Prosecution is in a luxurious position because we have not received a paginated version. Let's see, page 29, the 15th of March commences on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the records here reveal that the paginated version, the first page is page 10534 and if we can just do a simple addition --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure you can, Mr. Margetts. Your Honour, I have very limited time for cross-examination and I would be grateful if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. I'll find the relevant page. Mr. Margetts, does that mean that you have not the LiveNote version at all? It's available to the Prosecution as well, isn't it? On your computer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We do not have it with us, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not on your computers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll make the arithmetical calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do it as you wish. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now when you were giving evidence on Tuesday, Mr. Djokanovic, you indicated you were giving some evidence in relation to decision makers in relation to Mr. Karadzic, Professor Koljevic, Professor Plavsic, and Mr. Krajisnik, and you were giving them a ranking in terms of one to four; you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And also in relation to this -- you were also giving evidence in relation to the influence of various people. That was at page 32 of the LiveNote transcript for the benefit of Court and counsel. You recall giving that evidence in relation to political influence. I think Judge Hanoteau asked you some questions about what you meant by influence. You recall all of that, of course?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you also gave some evidence in relation to the position of Speaker of the Assembly or President of the Assembly being the second most important position in the state and that was at page 34 of the LiveNote transcript. And you recall, of course, giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I think that you were asked about this question of influence at page 36 of the transcript from Tuesday, and Judge Hanoteau asked you a question about where does this power, where does this influence come from, in essence. And your answer was: "From the ignorance and the mediocrity of those who accept that, Your Honours." You recall that answer, of course. Mr. Djokanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, of course, but I would like to add a few sentences at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Djokanovic, what I'm going to do is ask you a few more questions and I'll then invite you after I finish with the matters that I need to deal with to add a few points, Mr. Djokanovic. Now, firstly, in terms of the Speaker's roles and powers, you are aware, of course, that the duties of the President of the Assembly or the Speaker of the Assembly is that he presides over the Assembly sessions; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And he allows various politicians to speak in order; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And matters are proposed for voting by the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in essence, of course the Speaker himself only has one vote?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, too, is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it does not.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the question is missing on page 6, line 2, where the witness answered of course it does not. The question disappears.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question. There's no need -- I take it if you put the same question, we expect the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course the Speaker does not have a casting vote. That was that question where it wasn't recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered that already. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in relation to that question, the Speaker, of course, does not control the agenda. He has to put forward whatever is put forward by the various Deputies' Clubs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And he has to present these matters on the agenda whether he agrees with them or not; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course in terms of the way that we look at the parliamentary system in both Bosnia-Herzegovina and the separate Serbian Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were different state functions. You look at the Presidency, the Assembly, and the government. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in relation, for example, on the 14th and 15th of October, 1991, when the independence proposal was put forward by the Bosnian Muslim and the Bosnian Croatian politicians, Mr. Krajisnik of course had to put that on the agenda because that was his role as a speaker; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, so in terms of this influence that you were talking about, and the power, you'd agree with me, would you not, that Mr. Krajisnik, in many ways, was perceived to be, in fact, more powerful than he was because he was on the television and the media a lot because the parliamentary sessions were constantly televised and, of course, as presiding over the Assembly, he got a lot of media coverage. You'd agree with that, would you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, these are five questions in one. Would you please split them up.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I'm more than happy to split them up. It's just that I'm very conscious of my limited time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But at the same time you suggested that it was perception by televisions which of course that some Members of Parliament would not only obtain knowledge of what happens in parliament -- or in the Assembly by television.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in terms of Mr. Krajisnik's generally perceived power and influence, a lot of that was due to the fact that the parliamentary sessions were televised and he got a lot of media coverage. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in relation to what you've said about the ranking of various people and their perceived influence, that, of course, is your view and of course you allow for the possibility that other people would -- could form different views?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's -- it's not very helpful to the Court for Mr. Djokanovic to speculate on what other people could possibly form views on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. It's not a matter of speculation. Ms. Loukas, it's whatever the witness answers. If he says: "You asked whether there's a possibility that other people would form different views. If it's witness says no, this doesn't mean that this is an answer one could logically accept. If the witness says yes, it is common knowledge because on every subject, other people can always take different views. So it's -- certainly I would agree with Mr. Margetts that it doesn't assist the Chamber. I mean, if I ask you whether I have a certain view on a certain matter, whether there's a possibility that someone else has a different view -- how could I ever exclude that other people have different views?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, one could not, Your Honour. But I would submit it is a proper matter for cross-examination. The witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we are not -- I mean, of course this Chamber is aware that if, in the context of questions on power not resulting just merely from official functions, but of course you could have different views on how far or how strong that power would be. That goes without saying. But please proceed. I just wanted to let you know that it's not -- your question was not asking for speculation, but the answer is yes, whatever the witness says, the possibility is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I take it that Your Honour is therefore prepared to make a finding at this point that these -- this evidence in relation to perceived influence and rankings in terms of position is merely this witness's view and of course other views are possible on the same evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course the Chamber will consider those matters in the context of all of the evidence presented and of course it's the view of this witness and either it finds support in other evidence or it's not supported by other evidence, and then finally, the Chamber will make the determinations it will have to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So Mr. Djokanovic, in terms of the opinions that you've expressed in relation to Mr. Krajisnik as a main decision-maker, that is purely and simply your view; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have asked me a couple of questions there. I will try to respond in a couple of sentences although it was all formulated as one question. Mr. Krajisnik was the President of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he was the second in rank in power, and this is a position that he inherited by inertia. His principle task entrusted him by the Serbian side was to prevent the passage of any document that would disrupt interethnic relations in Bosnia-Herzegovina which would be in contravention of the SFRY constitution and the B and H constitution and ultimately in the couldn't vision of the rules of procedure of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course he adhered to form and he never violated it, but he did not actually carry out his political task and that is a historical fact. However, he did not finish his political career by his defeat in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but he very carefully and systematically built his political image until the end of the war, so that the last amendments to the constitutions of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was quite clear. The President of the republic together with the President of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska, i.e., the president of the republic in consultation with the President of the Assembly of Republika Srpska was the one to appoint the prime minister designate to actually form the government of Republika Srpska. So practically his activity as the President of the Assembly was, after all, defined under the constitution. On the eve of the war by forming this National Security Council [Realtime transcript read in error "National Council"], the influence of Professor Koljevic and Professor Plavsic who, in the '90s had been elected in a democratic way to the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina actually failed to third place.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I really don't want to interrupt you there, but I have to explain to you that I have very limited time for questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I would -- it's our submission that the point at which counsel has interrupted the witness is the very point that was the butt of her question, and we'd suggest that it be appropriate for the witness to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness may finish his answer although he should be aware that -- not to take too much time. The last part of your answer was about the activity of Mr. Krajisnik as the President of the Assembly as defined under the constitution, and that on the eve of war by forming this National Council, the influence of Professor Koljevic and Professor Plavsic who, in the '90s had been elected in a democratic way to the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina actually failed to third place. Could you finish what you were telling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a correction on the transcript, Your Honour at page 10, line 20, there's a reference to the National Council. We heard it as the National Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you finish that answer and at the same time, keep in mind that time is limited.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the name is council for national security, yes. It was referred to at the session of the National Assembly at Pale, I believe, on the 24th of March. There was a proposal to appoint Dr. Karadzic as president of the council. The second place was to go to you were telling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a correction on the transcript, Your Honour at page 10, line 20, there's a reference to the National Council, we heard it as the National Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you finish that answer and at the same time, keep in mind that time is limited.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the name is council for national security, yes. It was referred to in the session of the National Assembly at Pale, I believe, on the 24th of March, there was a proposal to appoint Dr. Karadzic as president of the council. The second place was to go to the President of the Assembly of the Serbian People, and the third to the member of the Presidency. So I objected. I asked why they were doing this because they -- I thought that this was yet a step further towards making the situation even more illegitimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, just on that point about the National Security Council, of course there was a debate about that as you've just referred to in Pale on the 24th of March, 1992 and you'd agree with me, would you not, that in relation to that issue, Mr. Krajisnik took the same view that you did, that it would merely be a consultative body; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik adopted the same position as I myself and all this was postponed by several days, so I lost sight of the further activities of this council; in fact, I thought that it will never been actually established. But after I came to Pale from Belgrade, I could see that this Presidency hierarchy that I found at Pale actually reflected the relations that I spoke about in my previous statement. President Karadzic was man number one and -- in the Presidency, and Mr. Krajisnik was almost on an equal footing as Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic wielded significant influence in that period, but certainly second to that of Mr. Krajisnik. That is my opinion and I also believe that many people share this view of mine, especially those people who came to Pale on any business whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Djokanovic, I understand that this is your view but you, of course, can see that not everybody held the same view as you; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not, so far, heard a different opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, you're not seriously telling the Court that another view is not possible, are you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I just said that until now, I haven't heard or read that anyone said that Mr. Krajisnik was not second in influence after Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you'd agree with me assessments of this nature are necessarily impressionistic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, the witness has been asked to contemplate matters of psychology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, this witness has told us that he had not heard any other view. There's nothing impressionistic about that. That's just a fact, whether you heard that or not. Ask one additional question. Mr. Djokanovic, you said, "And I also believe that many people shared this view of mine." At the same time that you said that you did not hear any other view. Did these other people, these many people, did they express to you explicitly that they were of that view, that they shared your view, or was it just that they did not express any other view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I never heard from a single personality in the area who might say that Mr. Krajisnik was -- wielded much less influence than Mr. Karadzic. In fact, it was the generally shared view in the territory of the Serbian republic that he was as influential as Karadzic if not more so in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That still does not answer my question because you told us already that you did not hear any different opinion. What I asked you is whether people explicitly expressed to you that they shared your views either in factual terms or in their assessment of the power of Mr. Krajisnik. So that no one said something different is clear to me now, but did they in a positive way say, This is how we look at it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Koljevic, in those days, spoke to me explicitly about the situation in the Presidency and the influence of Mr. Krajisnik. Mrs. Plavsic spoke along the same lines. And certain people who were commissioners, such as Mr. Poplasen and Mr. Radovanovic, Mr. Vucabic [phoen], all of them discussed the issue with me and they all agreed that Mr. Krajisnik, next to Mr. Karadzic, was the most influential person. And when I say "influential," influential over the deputies, the political situation, and also when it came to making important decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, just in relation to this question of Mr. Krajisnik's influence, I put it to you, Mr. Djokanovic, that what you're saying is just not true.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are being remunerated to defend your client.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Djokanovic, I think that that sort of comment is thoroughly inappropriate, and I'm sure the Trial Chamber would agree with me that that sort of answer is completely inappropriate from a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, Ms. Loukas puts it to you that what you said is not true. Rather than to comment on why she puts this to you, the Chamber would like you to answer the question. So whether you agree with her or you disagree with her or whatever shade of grey is between black and white.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Loukas said that I was not telling the truth. I am telling the truth and nothing but the truth, and I took an oath to that effect at the beginning. Ms. Loukas is entitled to present all arguments in -- to contradict my statements and my comments, and it is up to the Trial Chamber to weigh both and to tell me -- but rather than telling me that I'm not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, there might be some misunderstanding with the witness if you are not used to the -- I would say to the techniques of the examination-in-chief and cross-examination, putting something to a witness, it might confuse a witness. I do understand from his answer that he disagrees with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, and I can understand that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, let's get one thing straight here, okay? Firstly, the whole thing here is to find the truth; you understand that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And neither you or I are going to make the ultimate decision; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course that entire process of justice, as you understand it, is that both sides get to present their perspective and the Trial Chamber ultimately determines; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So I'd be grateful if you could assist me in that process of finding the truth by answering my questions and not making comments. Do we understand each other?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think everyone in the courtroom noticed that yesterday, I provided very brief answers to all questions without wishing to waste any of your time. That is my intention still. However, there's not -- no reason why I shouldn't comment on certain things if I feel I have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, you certainly can comment on the subject matter of questions but you are supposed not to comment on why a question is put to you, whether Ms. Loukas is -- whether it's her duty, whether she fulfills her duty, that's not something we need any comment on. At the same time, Ms. Loukas, I think the witness in his previous answer sufficiently made that clear that he understands what we are doing here.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, and I'm happy to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the evidence you've given, Mr. Djokanovic, that you were answerable to Mr. Krajisnik in relation to War Commissions from July 1992 and specifically in relation to Novo Sarajevo, I put to you that that's not true. You can answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true what you have just said because Mr. Branko Radan, after talking to me, went to see Mr. Krajisnik and agreed with him that I should come to Novo Sarajevo to assist them in nominating municipal commissioners.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness approach the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please come a bit closer to the microphone. Perhaps, Madam Usher, you could assist. May I just ask for one clarification, Mr. Djokanovic. Ms. Loukas asked you whether or not your answer about Mr. Krajisnik in relation to War Commissions and specifically in relation to Novo Sarajevo. In your answer, you explain that you were sent to Novo Sarajevo after Mr. Radan had consulted Mr. Krajisnik and had agreed with Mr. Krajisnik, but being answerable is not exactly the same as being sent after a consultation with. I mean, the next step is what do you do when you went to Novo Sarajevo and to who do you report back. So the answer - but perhaps, Ms. Loukas, you could pursue the matter - does not exactly fit to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm going to move on to another topic and come back to that one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, in your evidence on Tuesday, you gave evidence in relation to telling Mr. Krajisnik and various members of the leadership about certain matters. Now, when we were going through your statement yesterday, you agreed that what you'd told the investigators was that you conveyed general information about the situation and the places I had visited to the War Presidency informing them that "many bad things happened." And of course that was a matter that was also dealt with in court yesterday at page 54. And your answer was: "Yes, that bad things, ugly things were happening in the field and that they looked like war crimes. I was quite clear in what I said. I said that action needed to be taken. That we needed to organise a meeting with those people as soon as possible to see what was actually happening in the field." That was your answer in relation to this question of reporting when I was asking you about your statement. You agree with that, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in answer to His Honour's question on Tuesday --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, if I might have a moment. I'm just looking for the particular page reference. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give us the literal text, we will be able to find it in a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. It was page 73, Your Honours, of Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, your response in relation to a question from the Presiding

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WAS THAT
utterances.text: "And that's what you told the members of the Presidency upon your return to Pale, that people were killed and driven out on a mass scale and that was the information you got. Is that a correct understanding?" And you said in response to that question to the Presiding Judge that: "Yes, you have understood me precisely." You recall that interchange, Mr. Djokanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I remember. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And yet at the same time, in cross-examination, you agree that what you basically said was that many bad things happened; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Djokanovic, it seems to me -- or I put it to you that as a witness, you tend to give the answer that you think your audience wants?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: My learned friend is juxtaposing the evidence that Dr. Djokanovic gave yesterday and I'd invite her to describe fully that evidence and that evidence in part was to adopt the statement that he provided and that statement provides a more detailed description of matters that were reported than my learned friend has, in fact, put in her question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether there is a sound basis for your question, Ms. Loukas, is another matter, but you put it to the witness. Mr. Djokanovic, Ms. Loukas puts it to you that you give the answers you imagine those who are questioning you would like to hear. That's what she puts to you and you may respond to that position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. When Mrs. Malone at the beginning of 2003 started talking to me about the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period from 1990 to 1992, she told me at the very beginning that the investigators were fully aware of my activities in that period of time, that I was absolutely clean in all that, and she told me at the very beginning that I didn't have to give statements to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal if I don't wish to. I told Mrs. Malone that due to various circumstances, I happened to have such a role in that -- those turbulent times and that in my opinion, it is a duty of a witness of the time to testify. And when in December, 2003, we were completing my second statement here in The Hague, only upon the end of that statement was the name mentioned as to whose trial I might appear at. And I told Mr. Margetts, who was talking to me at the time, and his colleague whose name I can't recall, I inquired about him, I was told he went to the United States, and I said that we haven't discussed names and now suddenly a name has cropped up, and I would have one request to make: May I be a witness of the Court rather than a witness of the Prosecution. That was my question. And I was told with precision that they would have consultations and they would let me know the next day. The next day, I was told that there had been certain precedents to the effect that some people had been granted such a status but as for my case, there was no need to decide in that way because I was just expected to be a witness of the truth, not the witness of the Prosecution or the Defence or the Trial Chamber, but a witness of the truth, and I accepted that. And then they asked me in connection with protective measures. I said that there was no need for any protective measures because I was ready to speak about this in court and in public, and that is why I said that there was no need for protective measures. And when I returned home that I would send a fax to that effect. And after the new year holidays, I did send this fax message saying that I would speak clearly in public and frankly about everything I knew, that I didn't need any protective measures. My statement may be of assistance to someone, it may have the opposite effect, too, but that is life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the last answer has been finished so --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I was waiting for the last answer to finish, Your Honour. I thought that there was still interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I didn't notice interpretation. But the last lines were, "My statement may be of assistance to someone, it may have the opposite effect too, but that is life."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, you, of course, have never said anything like, We should go to war, have you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are you referring to in connection with my statement and words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I may have said it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Would you -- you certainly would never have said anything like that in a political debate, would you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout that period, 1991, 1992, and this is clear from all my public statements and speeches in the Assembly, I always favoured attempts to find the best solution by peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So in terms of your political stance, it was always, We should not go to war. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every possible -- all possible means should be sought to avoid war.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That was always your position; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my position from the moment I appeared on the political stage until the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course that was the position that you took in political debates in the Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That was the position that you took when you attended SDS Deputy Club meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend deputy club meetings of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So on the 18th of October, 1991, you did not attend a SDS Deputies' Club meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are probably talking about members of the Serbian deputies who left the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina to discuss the possibility of forming the Assembly of the Serbian People. I probably did attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, of course, this was just after the 14th and 15th of October, 1991; correct? Those tumultuous days of the 14th and 15th of October, 1991, all the Serb deputies got together to have a meeting, did they not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And there was a meeting on the 18th of October, 1991, correct, which you attended?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I think that in that period of time, I attended all meetings held in Sarajevo of deputies, consultations on multi-party cooperation, a narrow group of people in the office of the President of the Assembly, so it's quite possible, but I don't remember precisely which that meeting you are referring to was.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the Court, I'm about to refer to P65, folder 3, tab 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed..

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just to prompt your memory, Mr. Djokanovic, it was held in the Blue Hall of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, does that prompt your memory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, -- there was no meetings in that period of time that I did not attend but as there was so many, I can't remember exactly. I do remember a meeting between the time the deputies walked out of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the constitution of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that meeting was in the Blue Hall, if that's the one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, if the document might be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, if you look at that document, Mr. Djokanovic, you'll see that you're noted as speaking at point 28. Do you have the relevant portion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do you want to read out to the Court what you say there? Will you please read that out to the Court?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is what it says here: "Dr. Djokanovic, the 28th in order. Had we had a plebescite three months ago, things would be easier now. They don't have a constitution. The Serbian people must vote for the constitution of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think we should go to war right away." That is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, so you agree with me you're recorded as saying, "We should go to war right away." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says here, but my overall political activities show that these were not my sentences. At the very next Assembly meeting at the constituent meeting of the Assembly of the Serbian People, a number of deputies spoke about war, but reason prevailed and the position was that a political solution should be sought. A single word could be left out to change the whole meaning. Maybe I actually said, I don't think we should go to war, just to make it negative. And Mr. Toholj [phoen] on one occasion when we met in Belgrade, when we spoke about those times, he said, We've cleaned it all. What had they cleaned? What documents were they referring to when saying that they had cleaned it? And also I noticed in a number of other places in the minutes of Assembly meetings that some things had been slightly changed. I must say slightly.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... agree with me you're recorded as saying "We should go to war right away," correct? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the question has been answered where the witness said that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, I mean, he accepts that his words have been recorded in this document as saying, "I think we should go to war right away." And then next, he explained that this could not be his words and he gives an explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then he supports that by he referring to his overall political attitude.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But just to avoid whatever misunderstanding had -- from your explanation, should I conclude that it is still possible that you've spoken those words or that you even have spoken them or do you say: No, it must be a misrecording?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was probably a misrecording. It was inadvertent, perhaps. The only way the sentence could he had read is that I do not think we should immediately go to war. And it was obviously in the ensuing sessions of the Assembly that I was always advocating a peaceful solution of the problems in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that there was light at the end of the tunnel, and that we should pursue that kind of an end, in this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, I just want to go back to your proofing session with Mr. Margetts. You told us in court that you had certain matters that you thought needed correction in your statement and you told Mr. Margetts about it. That's basically the position, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a couple of things which did not change anything in terms of substance but were commented upon. In fact, I did not even insist on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Nevertheless, of course the lawyers from the Prosecution noted down what you were saying when you were talking to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I wasn't aware, actually, of the -- that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, obviously when the lawyers are with you in a proofing session, Mr. Djokanovic, they have pen and paper and they're taking notes of what you're saying; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he talked to me, Mr. Margetts always had a pen and a notebook of course, but we discussed so many things. My account was very exhaustive so it is indeed difficult to put on paper everything, everything that I say. I never set great store by that because I knew that if I appeared in court one day that that would be the moment where I would say what I had to say, that the courtroom was the venue to discuss all these things in detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Are you saying Mr. Margetts was not taking notes when you indicated there were slight changes from your statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. What I said was that I didn't know what it was that Mr. Margetts was putting down. As far as I can recall, he was jotting down what we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course when you told him there were changes, he was taking notes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the witness said that during his conversations with Mr. Margetts, Mr. Margetts was taking notes. He had a pen in front of him and a piece of paper, so that's -- that question has been answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it's a little unfortunate that Mr. Margetts is actually the person doing the objection in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with you that that's an unfortunate situation. Mr. Margetts, could I ask you to not object unless -- of course this objection was a question asked and question answered issue which is a relatively neutral issue even if the question was about Mr. Margetts. But may I give you the guidance that to the extent necessary, even if the question has been asked and answered, then it's not dramatic if the question would be put again and perhaps you -- your position at this moment to ask for some -- well, not stepping back, but perhaps to go down to the -- what really is basically needed for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I could suggest possibly that Mr. Harmon could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If Mr. Harmon feels that he is in a position that he can take over, then on this -- on objections, that would certainly be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But of course Ms. Loukas I should have asked you first because it's not usual that another counsel takes over on a specific part.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I think it's appropriate at this moment that Mr. Djokanovic remove his headphones. There is just a matter I want to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I try to resolve the matter. You repeatedly said that you have not much time.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I heard questions like, Is it true that the 18th of October, 1991, is a couple of days after the 14th of October. Even this Chamber is in the position to, if something happens on the 18th of October, that knowing what happened on the 14th and the 15th, there's really no need to -- but -- he has taken off his earphones already. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The point I want to make is this, and this is why I've asked Mr. Djokanovic to take off his headphones. What is emerging, of course, is a credit issue between Mr. Margetts and the witness. This, of course, is rather unfortunate, but it places the Defence in the position of perhaps having to call Mr. Margetts in relation to the question of the witness's credit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether that would help us out. But of course if any such a request will be put before this Chamber, we'll decide on it. At the same time ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The importance and relevance of the issue is limited in view of the changes made. Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In view of the ... Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the changes in the statement we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is a matter that goes to the credit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, the importance and relevance is limited, I said. I did not say that it's irrelevant. I did not say that it had no importance at all but -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Now, if Mr. Djokanovic might have his headphones reinserted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, in relation to your relationship with Mr. Krajisnik, if I can put it that way --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If Mr. Djokanovic might be shown his second statement of 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The page in English would be, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The page in English, Your Honour, would be page 10. That's the December statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in B/C/S, that would be ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: We're just checking with the interpreter now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, you have your statement before you, page 10 in the English and we're just checking the B/C/S paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I'm not -- of course I'm not a native speaker but if it would be in page 11, it would not surprise me. The bottom of page 10 in English and -- in the middle of page 11 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I see. So yes, it starts at the bottom of page 10 in the B/C/S and continues on page 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Do you have that before you, Mr. Djokanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have pages 10 and 11 before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, in that paragraph, have you read through it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking the -- about the last paragraph on page 10 in which then goes on on page 11; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Have you read through that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So that is talking about the time when -- well, in fact, the previous paragraph as well. You might want to have a look at that previous paragraph as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're having some difficulty locating the paragraph that Ms. Loukas is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: English text is last three digits ERN is 185 and on that page is the second and the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So, yes, in the English on page 10, it's the second full paragraph. I'm now referring to the first full paragraph and the second full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Djokanovic, if you can have a look at both of those paragraphs. Have you read them both?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I've also read the one before.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So what we've got there is that you say that Djeric, Mr. Branko Djeric asked you to become a member of the government; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And then you give the opinion that: "Someone obstructed the voting so that I did not become a member of the government." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And then your very next sentence is: "At this time, Mr. Krajisnik had established his position very firmly." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So what you say is that you hold Mr. Krajisnik responsible for you not becoming a member of the government; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, I do not hold him responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, let's look a little bit further down in that paragraph. You said that: "It was possible for the prime minister to suggest that I should become his minister and the Assembly rejects that." Do you see that portion there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you say: "They could not do it openly. They could not vote me out openly because they did not have firm arguments against me, however, they created the situation where they did not have enough people to vote." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says here. These are my answers to a number of the investigator's questions. So the entire story actually latches on to my talks with Mr. Djeric regarding the situation in Zvornik. When Mr. Branko Djeric, who was the first prime minister of the Serbian republic, when he heard that Brano Grujic had attacked me at the previous meeting, he said, I was accused of war crimes by Alija Izetbegovic and now I'm being accused by our own official Dragan Djokanovic for these very same things. This talk with Mr. Djeric took place in the Kikinda building where the Presidency was, and Mr. Djeric and I talked in some detail about certain issues and after he had offered me a member -- a position on the government, I asked him, Mr. Djeric, do you really want the government to control more space than only the parking lot in the front of the Bistrica hotel at Mount Jahorina? And he said Yes. So I asked him, Are you ready to crack down on crime which is being increasingly talked about? And Mr. Djeric responded, Yes, then you can count on my support. I will accept to be a member of your government. Although we did not talk about the specific department. And, I will try to elicit the support of the members of the Presidency, and I'm quite sure that you will have the support of two Presidency members. And I was talking about Mr. Koljevic and Ms. Plavsic at that time. So this is the subject that we were discussing, and I also reckoned that I would be able to ensure the support, the sure support of Biljana Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic because we had already talked about problems in the field and the crime before that and I knew what their position was. But I was also counting on this fact: That if Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic so opted that Mr. Karadzic would also accept it. Truth to tell, I did not count on Krajisnik's support knowing that he was in close ties with two ministers who, in that period, were actually the ones at whom the finger was being pointed the most, that was Mr. Mandic, the minister of justice, and the interior minister, the minister of the police, Mr. Stanisic. That summer, at the Assembly meeting in the Bijeljina which I did not attend, but let me describe the political situation that reigned at the time. The prime minister was unable to form a cabinet at that time, the Assembly actually elected individual --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's not answering my question. Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Mr. Djokanovic, let me just reread your question, exactly, Ms. Loukas, so that we ... The answer at least was that long that it is not on our screen anymore. The quote put to you was: You say they could not do it openly. They could not vote me out openly because they did not have firm arguments against me. However, they created the situation where they did not have enough people, I think it says, to vote. Ms. Loukas, you're asking the witness whether this is correct. You put five, six or seven elements to him and say if it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It is a quotation, Your Honour, from his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But -- well, if the witness -- I think that witness thinks that it needs more explanation because that would -- otherwise there would be no need to put that question to him. So therefore, if you would have more precise answers, you are invited to put more -- less complex questions to him. Because you could have split it up. You could have said openly, why not openly? Or is that true? The second is the firm arguments, what arguments might there have been. I mean, then we come to the core. But if you give him a full range of -- I see you're looking at the clock, please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The only reason I'm looking at the clock is because I'm going to run out of time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I give you an opportunity to -- where I give you the guidance that if you put questions in a different way, you more easily get the answer instead of the witness not knowing exactly what to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's a balancing exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please take your time to put the questions to the witness rather than to debate with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm happy to continue with the questioning on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, getting back to your statement, Mr. Djokanovic, you say there: "They could not do it openly. They could not vote me out openly because they did not have firm arguments against me. However, they created the situation where they did not have enough people to vote." Who is the "they"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This specifically refers to the entire Assembly of the Serbian People because what I talked about in relation to the problems in Zvornik was a non-political issue among the politicians in the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. So if I were to become a minister that summer, and Mr. Djeric wanted me to become one and some of the deputies actually stated positive views on my appointment - in fact, some of them voted for my becoming a minister - that would mean affirming what I was saying at that time, namely, that the prime minister should form his cabinet, should be answerable for his work, that the government should do its work in keeping with the constitution and that would mean asserting me as a person who was talking about war crimes in that period. It is well known in politics if one talks about these issues, one actually is nominating oneself to actually work in that particular department, and by saying this, I was actually nominating my own self to work in the department of the rule of law and the activities to be undertaken by the Republika Srpska in addressing the issue of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's have a look at the next paragraph, all right? You've got in relation to this issue about you becoming a minister: "However, instead of voting immediately a break was called and when the members returned, there was no longer a quorum and the vote could not take place." Now, the person of course who called the break was Mr. Krajisnik, correct, because he was the Speaker. We are in agreement there, are we not, Mr. Djokanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at that Assembly session but I -- but knowing what had transpired there, I was told what had happened, I asked the person from the Presidency to give me a couple of pages from the stenogramme which referred to precisely that issue. I believe I have given the investigators this document. If not, I have it here -- not here in the courtroom but I do have it. Needless to say, I also listened to the audiotape recording of the Assembly session and I could see that something unusual was happening in the conference room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, the question put to you whether you agree with Ms. Loukas that it was Mr. Krajisnik who called the break. So either you agree or you disagree. If further explanation is needed, Ms. Loukas will certainly ask for it. Please proceed. Perhaps first, on the basis of what you saw in these pages of the transcript, do you agree with Ms. Loukas that it was Mr. Krajisnik who called for the break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik chaired the Assembly session. It was up to him to adjourn or to reconvene the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you do agree. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, you blame Mr. Krajisnik for not becoming a minister, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle here, I'm just describing the situation that obtained in the Assembly, I do not even know whether Mr. Krajisnik voted in favour or against, at all. I do not know how he opted and I do not blame him for whatever position he took.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... two paragraphs of your statement talking about this issue. Do you see that, Mr. Djokanovic? You agree with me, don't you, that you spent two paragraphs of your statement talking about this issue of you not becoming a minister?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, an entire statement would have been necessary here to describe that entire period because that was a period when I knew policy could have emerged inside the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is not only associated with my own involvement and work in the government, it is also associated with that but it is -- it has to do about with Mr. Djeric's remaining and forming cabinet as someone who is capable to actually grapple with matters at hand and someone who was ready to grapple with all the difficult problems. It was a very difficult period and to my surprise and to the surprise of all well-meaning people. Already the next session which was in Zvornik, Mr. Djeric had to tender in his resignation.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, I put to you that you bear a grudge against Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik and I had correct communication throughout that period while I was minister, and after the war I was once at Pale and he was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and before that, he had gone to see my parents which actually I thought was very nice of him. So after that, I returned this visit and we talked and we had a very pleasant conversation and there were no tensions of any kind between me and Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, you're biased against Mr. Krajisnik because you hold him responsible for not becoming a minister; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did become a minister later on. I consider Mr. Krajisnik as a politician to be responsible because he wasn't fully concentrated and in the memorandum about Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was a politician that the people had a great deal of regard for and he could have done much more than he actually did, than what happened. But that is just my political opinion about that Assembly meeting. When talking about that, I think there are very -- various views as to Mr. Krajisnik could have done more or not. I personally think he could have. I think he was much more capable than he demonstrated that evening but the things you said absolutely don't stand because I became a minister a couple of months later. I mention this just as a detail which could have marked the beginning of a new policy and I think we would have all fared better and there would have been no trial at The Hague, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Djokanovic, it's now time for the break and I'm about to move on to a new topic so I'll continue my questioning after the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I do understand that you'd like to respond to the request in respect of protective measures in view of Witness KRAJ 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm entirely in Your Honour's hands whether it's dealt with right now or -- whatever is more convenient for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not know whether you wanted to stay or whether you wanted to leave so I would like to give you an opportunity right now and that's reason why --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we could do it in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I say straight away that I was -- I did propose to make some introductory remarks on this issue which wouldn't require private session but at the point where it requires private session then of course conscientiously to draw attention to that and ensure that we don't trespass on ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, how much time do you think you would need for both introductory remarks and -- I'm just asking your assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I really don't think I'm going to need more than about five minutes for each, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's quite a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't quite catch what Your Honour said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said that's quite a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ten minutes, Your Honour. Yes, that's my assessment

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed and try to keep it as brief as possible. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was -- I was told that we would proceed with this issue afterwards. Mr. Gaynor is going to deal with that issue. I just excused Mr. Gaynor two minutes ago so I can call him down to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The reason why that I wanted to deal with it right away is that I did not want to put Mr. Stewart in a position where he had to wait for an hour and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may -- may -- may I -- my -- my -- my point in some conversation before Your Honour came in, my point was that I did come down now specifically this -- for this but on the other hand, Your Honour, I am proposing to stay for this session so I'm totally -- I appreciate Your Honour's concern for my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait -- then we'll wait until a later moment because that was the one and only reason why I did not want to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, I had come down in accordance with the arrangements agreed the other day but I'm -- I'm -- I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wouldn't miss it for the world, Your Honour, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, Ms. Loukas will continue cross-examination. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, let's go back to some evidence you were giving just prior to the break. And it's at page 35, line 8 for the benefit of the Court and counsel. And that is that you were saying that, in essence, this specifically refers to the entire Assembly session, Assembly of the Serbian People because what I talked about in relation to the problems in Zvornik was a non-political issue among the politicians in the Serbian -- in the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, so if I were to become a minister that summer and Mr. Djeric wanted me to become one and some of the deputies actually stated positive views on my appointment, in fact some of them voted for my becoming a minister, that would mean affirming what I was saying at that time, namely that the prime minister should form this cabinet, should be answerable for his work, that the government should do its work in keeping in the constitution and that would be asserting me as a person who was talking about war crimes in that period." Now, you remember that evidence you just gave before the break, Mr. Djokanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, you are, of course, putting yourself forward as somebody who, during that period, we're talking about from June onwards, is a person who was talking about war crimes; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period of time, I was talking about War Commissions, but what I saw in the field I conveyed to members of the Presidency and I spoke about it with the prime minister. That situation should have prompted everyone to do something. I did what I did, what I could as far as my possibilities allowed and the influence I wielded and I had considerable influence, especially as I cooperated very well with members of the Presidency. Dr. Koljevic and Dr. Plavsic so in that period of time, I was highly influential and initiating a new kind of policy in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Djokanovic, you, during that period, are now putting yourself forward as some sort of war crimes hero, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't put it like that. I tried, as I have explained, I wanted a new executive body to be formed which would act in accordance with the constitution with respect to war crimes and general crime that was being talked about among the people. The fact -- it is a fact that I spoke about it and I didn't avoid coming to grips with such a problem, and Mr. Djeric offered me the position of minister for questions of veterans and victims of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, the fact is you were not talking to everybody you could in that period from June onwards about war crimes, were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to people who -- close by, with people that I thought could effect a change.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, one of the organs in our society that can effect a change is, of course, the media. Did you speak to the media about what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I didn't feel that all possibilities had been exhorted been the political establishment of the Serbian republic. I believe that if I had the support of members of the Presidency, that is Koljevic and Plavcic for a new policy, and also from the prime minister, especially as he was the first prime minister, I thought that many things could be achieved through the institutions. I was always aware that there was no statute of limitations for war crimes so there would be time to talk about that in the media too, but I did everything I could through the institutions of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to have a state system developed. I must say that this was a period of time when all the state elements were not fully functional, and my policy was based on the constitution of civilian authorities in the municipalities to have vertical communication between the municipalities and the Presidency for the Assembly and the government to play their part in accordance with the constitution and that all this should be in accordance with our policies. I had only two pieces of paper in my pocket for this trial which I thought was important and that is an original minutes from a meeting. I think you have that among the documents. The proclamation to the peoples and citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina dated the 5th of November, 1991. When we called on all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina to take part in the plebescite and vote in favour of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. This doesn't appear to be an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am answering your question. In that proclamation, and I have the original signature of Dr. Karadzic, and he agrees with my initiative that we call on all the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina to vote for remaining in Yugoslavia. So Serb policy was very clear in that respect. We all wanted to go to the plebescite so that we would remain in Yugoslavia. The Serbs did not want to live alone. And we also had the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, if I understand Ms. Loukas well, then she was mainly saying that the last part of your answer was not an answer to her question anymore. But I take it, Ms. Loukas, that the beginning of the answer was in response of your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm just checking my question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question was about the -- you started saying the media could have affected and whether he did go to the media and then he explained why he did not. That he did not and why he did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. But now I think we've moved on to the plebescite of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That seems to be rather far away from ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Djokanovic, you were a person, and you've given evidence of this, who thought that Mr. Krajisnik's reliance on the constitution and the legality of the Assembly process on the 14th and 15th of October, 1991, was not enough; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His engagement at the time was not sufficient, but that is not important in my opinion. I wanted to tell you that we wanted to develop a healthy environment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You can either agree or disagree with my proposition. I don't have a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I have answered that question. Mr. Krajisnik, that night, respected the form. He fully respected the constitution of the SFRY and the rules of procedure of the Assembly. That is quite clear. I have said that several times during my testimony. But as a politician, I said that he could have done even more in view of his abilities. That is my subjective opinion. But as I was saying, that was not important in my view. I wanted a legal environment to be created. And on the basis of that plebescite and on the constitution we proclaimed, we copied many paragraphs from the International Human Rights Charter, and we should have respected what was contained in our constitution and all the organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Now, please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if you ask a witness whether he is a person and whether he has given evidence of this who thought something, then you are asking about whether he's a person and whether he gave evidence on it and then it's also on the subject matter. I mean, you can't blame the witness for not saying yes or no to that. Is he a person, did he give evidence on it, he might be a person but not have given evidence on it, he might have given evidence on it but wrongly. You are putting questions in such a way that you should not be surprised that the witness takes a bit more time, and you are certainly in a position to avoid that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not accept that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, nevertheless, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I wasn't asking the witness if he was a person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's what your question says.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then just -- that's what the transcript says. Let me then say the following. "In any event, Mr. Djokanovic, you were a person, and you have given evidence of this who thought that Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The person who thought, yes, that continues. It's the same thought, Your Honour, through the thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you say he was -- he has thoughts and has given evidence on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct. That he gave evidence of what his thoughts were at the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed and not lose more time.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
