utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, the situation is that your view is that Mr. Krajisnik should have gone beyond parliament and to a press conference and extra-parliamentary demonstrations; correct? That is your evidence, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have discussed this. I wouldn't place further emphasis on this. Mr. Krajisnik respected the form that evening. My opinion as a participant, and I have already said in court that he did not avail himself of all the possibilities. There were other democratic possibilities, demonstrations, press conferences, to inform the people and the international public what was being prepared in the Assembly. He kept quiet about that and that is what I'm reproaching him for. But I don't think that this should give the impression that I have anything against Mr. Krajisnik. It's something I absolutely wish to avoid. That is not true. Mr. Krajisnik and I, as I was saying, had very correct communication between us, and whatever I did in that period was to contribute to peace and respect the constitution. It says: "Human rights and freedoms. The citizen of Republika Srpska are equal in freedoms, rights, and duties before the law. They enjoy equal legal protection regardless of ethnicity ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, listening to your answer, it seems that you confirm that is what your evidence. That's what Ms. Loukas asked you. Please proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, and I'm talking her about June 1992, all right? You kept quiet about war crimes, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about it where I could with people in Zvornik, cautioning them clearly that they might be held responsible tomorrow. I spoke about it with members of the Presidency. Of course I didn't broadcast it. I believe that all these people were sufficiently intelligent. In a few sentences, I made myself quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, you didn't go to the media about war crimes in June 1992, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the possibility to talk about it in the media. I was at Pale and the only media was the television of Republika Srpska, which was in embryo form at the time, and it was our service, a service of the Presidency. So I didn't see any need for me to go on television when I thought it was up to the Presidency, the legal bodies to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: How about newspapers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any. I could have gone to Sarajevo, that's true.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Ms. Loukas please repeat the question, we didn't hear it because of the overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you are invited to repeat your question because of the overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: How about -- [B/C/S on English channel].

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Glas Podrinja is a local newspaper from Sabac. And when I was in Zvornik, a journalist from that newspaper came to talk to me and I have kept that interview. It's a local newspaper so I forgot to mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the -- [B/C/S on English channel]. [Previous translation continues] ... English but that has been restored. Your question was what Glas Podrinja was.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Exactly, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the question has been answered so you may move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, I show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I believe the Prosecution have been notified that I will be using this document, Your Honours, and I have copies for Your Honours and the registry in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And there's, in fact -- now, Mr. Djokanovic, you have before you an interview with you as republican commissioner for a number of municipalities of the Bihac region of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's a document you have before you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in that interview there's, of course, a photograph of you there, you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And of course when giving this interview you were telling the truth; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always spoke the truth. And this interview with journalist Petkovic, I have two comments to make. I did not authenticate this text. She spoke to me. She never showed it to me afterwards as we had agreed, and I searched for it for several months and I have kept this article to see what she wrote. And my second comment is I had some doubts when I saw her sitting with Marko Pavlovic about an hour after my conversation with her.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But of course, Mr. Djokanovic, you never asked for a correction at the time, did you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was published in the press, and talking to the investigators, I said that this was not for local paper in Bratunac. I didn't authorise it. There are a few words which were added and which changed the substance of my interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Djokanovic, the question you were asked by the journalist was this: "The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina made the coexistence of constitutive peoples almost impossible because peoples do not wish to live together as it is stressed more and more." Now, would you care to read out to the Court what you said in that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have a copy. Could it be placed under the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to my answer to the last question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, in view of the previous answer of the witness, you can invite him either to read what the newspaper says or to tell us what he said during the interview. You asked him to read what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's in view of the previous answer a too complex question. But of course we can read what is written down.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, this is what you said, according to the journalist Z. Petkovic: "In municipalities where the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is functioning, everybody is allowed free movement. That is the situation in the Serb municipality of Zvornik. Muslims who wish to go away and take refuge from the region which is, after all, endangered by the war are allowed to leave peacefully. Buses are provided from Zvornik, and everyone who wished to be transported to a destination in an organised way were allowed to do so. Most of them go to Subotica the right of every man is to protect his family. We confirm once again that the Serbs respect humanitarian principles and do not oppress anyone in the territories under their authority. Everything I say can be checked. Serbs care about peace very much and respect of the rights of all the peoples, even the right of the Serb people to have their own state, and to arrange it according to the law and democratically." Now, tell me, Mr. Djokanovic, what, about that answer do you not agree that you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think everything is correctly conveyed, but what is important is the following: My interview with this reporter was an interview after I had seen people from the Crisis Staff, so my comments are based on my conversations with people from the Crisis Staff and before I had spoken with certain citizens about the situation in Zvornik. So I came there with the platform of the commissions, and the reporter is talking about the platform and our policies. Never for a moment did I have any suspicions regarding the intentions of the local authorities to respect human rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you put your headphones on, you will hear it immediately from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, this interview is dated June the 25th; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was published by the newspaper on the 25th of June, but the actual interview took place on the day I came to Zvornik with the three documents. And the minute I arrived, I went to the municipal building and I barged into the Crisis Staff session. I told them that on coming to Zvornik, I could see old people crossing the bridge to Mali Zvornik and I asked them why are these people going there, and they told me they are probably seeking shelter with their in-laws and relatives in Mali Zvornik. And then I could see people leaving by buses to Subotica. So I mentioned all this in my interview with the journalist, trying to understand all this and to explain what I had seen with my very eyes why these people were crossing the bridge to go to Serbia. Namely, at that particular moment, I did not doubt for a minute the good intentions of the people in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, when you say you got further information later, Mr. Djokanovic, why didn't you contact the media after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I was saying, I had no possibility to talk to the media. This lady reporter is one that I knew from before. She used to work for Radio Zvornik, so we started talking on the subject spontaneously as it were. I did not seek out the journalist. I wanted to talk about it all when I returned to Pale with people in the Presidency. Why would I jump the gun and talk about it before talking to the people in headquarters? So I had the technical possibility to go to Belgrade and seek out the journalists of the different newspapers and talk to them about it but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, did you tell this journalist what they thought -- what you thought they wanted to hear?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the best thing if the original record of the interview with me was found. After we finished the interview, I saw this lady reporter in the company of Marko Pavlovic, a man from the Crisis Staff, not later than half an hour after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you told this journalist what you thought, I take it, she wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mainly told her what I wanted to say and to respond, of course, correctly to her questions. And I also expected the reporter to treat me in a fair fashion and to talk to me when preparing the actual text for the publishing, given the circumstances, rather than talk to Marko Pavlovic, a Crisis Staff member. I saw them talking on the balcony and I was suspicious, in fact, about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I do understand his answer to be that the witness, at that time, says he was not guided to please the journalist but rather to answer the questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, you're just not telling the truth about reporting war crimes, are you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not report the war crimes to the media. I didn't do it then, I would not do it now. It was much more logical for me - and I would do the same thing now - to go to the Presidency and talk about the issue with members of the Presidency. There is no doubt about that. I can answer all your questions with yes or no, but when we talk about such crucial issues, I have to give you an explanation. Simply we talked about it at Pale with all the members of the Presidency. I cannot recall whether Branko Djeric was there on the evening of the 16th, but if he wasn't, we talked about it, that is to say, he and I, alone, about this subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, may I ask you one thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness apparently understood your question about reporting war crimes as reporting to Pale. Is that what you meant? Then of course the question has been answered. If it was wider than -- you are just not telling the truth about reporting war crimes, are you? That was your question. And that followed immediately on all the press issues. But from his answer, he -- it appears that he understood your question as reporting to political figures or to -- well, at least not to the press. Is that what you meant, then the question has been answered. If you had something different to mind ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm talking about reporting to Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djokanovic, you could have done more than you did; that's correct, is it not, at the time, in relation to war crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could have done more. I certainly could have done more.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you didn't?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I did not know how to go about it at that time. Perhaps I was not aware of all the avenues available to me to make it public. Now, with hindsight, I'm aware that I could have done many other things, and I should have turned to the media and I could have done that, I think. I had ties -- the roads to Zvornik were clear, I could go to Belgrade and talk to the media there about it, but we had some business to finish in the leadership of Republika Srpska to form the new government after the resignation of Branko Djeric. And I was hoping that the new government would indeed pursue a new policy and that as a system we could counter war crimes. I didn't want any kind of publicity for myself or the halo of a hero, but I did want to grapple with these problems even though I was fully aware of how unpopular a job that was. And everyone who heard me talk about it knew that it was highly unpopular. It was much more popular to be an opportunist at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, you, in your interview and the two statements you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor and in your evidence in chief this week -- your evidence, your statements, are all coloured by the fact that you want to shift responsibility away from yourself as republican commissioner. And what I'm putting to you is this: Your efforts to put Mr. Krajisnik in the picture in relation to being informed about crimes and in relation to the War Commission, that is so you can ensure that you are not held responsible by giving the Prosecution what they want. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the interview with the Tribunal's investigators, I kept saying that I was a part of that leadership, that it was my life and that is something which still attends me today. I'm not talking about these things as about something peripheral and something that's that just so happened and I'm now remembering it. It is a part of me. Can you imagine what -- how it feels to be in a situation that I am in right now, that I am sitting here and my political ally and I would say my friend, Mr. Krajisnik, is sitting on the other side? Not for a single moment, never, at any time, did the -- and the investigators know this did I try to clear my name of anything or to justify my actions. I was a part of it. I was a part of that politics. I am trying to tell you what it was that I did and what it was that I wanted to do. If I bear any blame in all that, of course I will accept it. You ask me whether I could have done more. Now in hindsight I told you I could have done more, I should have done more, I really should have actually put my life at stake in order to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I have further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if your microphone would have been on, we would have heard that you had no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, before I finish, just to finalise under 90(H), I should also put that the evidence in relation to Mr. Krajisnik being part of the Presidency, Mr. Krajisnik being informed of crimes, Mr. Krajisnik's position of influence in the political hierarchy, and Mr. Krajisnik's position in relation to the war crimes, all these aspects of Mr. Djokanovic, you, Mr. Djokanovic, trying to put Mr. Krajisnik in the picture is just to get yourself out of the picture and save your own skin. That's what I'm putting to you, Mr. Djokanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you expect Mr. Djokanovic to answer to that at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm happy to -- I do expect him to answer it and -- Your Honour, I can indicate -- I can further add to the question:

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I take it that you would disagree with me, Mr. Djokanovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did my very best as much as I could within the system of Republika Srpska. When I saw that everything had been exhausted, I resigned and left the political scene. Of course I stayed on for a while because under the constitution, I had to continue doing that particular job for a while. But in respect of war crimes, I repeat, I should have done more then, already then, I should have. And you referred to the media. I should have gone to the media where I could have organised press conferences and talked on the subject. I should have also gone to the camp near Prijedor, at least tried to go there when I heard from the media that there existed one. I should have done all those things but I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, you did not discuss war crimes with Mr. Krajisnik. That's what I'm putting to you, and I take it that you disagree with me, and all I need is a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about these questions with Mr. Krajisnik and after all, we all had occasion to talk about it at a session of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Ms. Loukas, I, although I'm not have a common-law tradition, I always understood Rule 90(H) that you put to a witness the nature of the case for the party. You do that not at the very end of the questioning but somewhere when you confront him with the inconsistency of the answers he gave. But let's -- it's a technical matter which I'm glad to hear that I am wrong in understanding Rule 90(H).

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can indicate that in relation to that it's a matter purely within the per view of the advocate as to when the matter is put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even after he has said that has no further questions. I have some difficulties in putting that moment in part of the cross-examination. But let's not --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think it's a vital and important matter, but just perhaps at another moment, we might find a way how to deal exactly with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my only point is this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That when one is dealing with matters of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to ensure that in terms of 90(H) that I had crossed the Ts and dotted the Is, Your Honour, and that was my purpose. And I probably at that point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. I'm talking about the timing, but we don't have -- at this moment, it's not a matter which I would think that the Chamber would keep off from evaluating the evidence given by the witness under Rule 90(H).

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, indeed, Your Honour. But of course it's a rule of the Tribunal but it's important that we ensure as the Defence that we cannot be seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would rather not continue since we -- Mr. Margetts, do you have any questions in re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, yesterday you were asked by my learned friend in relation to the Crisis Staffs and their actions whether or not they wished to yield their authority anywhere else. And for the assistance of the Court and Defence, that's recorded at pages 57 to 58 of yesterday's transcript. In response to that, you said that in the municipalities you toured, they accepted the decisions to form commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Dr. Djokanovic could be shown his statements, both statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we have them nearby?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, instead of taking time with showing him the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What I will do is just read from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'm referring to page 15 of the English statement and the fifth paragraph and the first two sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First one or the second one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in your statement you said this, and I'm going to read it to you, and it will be translated to you and then I invite your comment as to whether or not you consider this accurate or not. You stated: "When I went to the municipalities, I presented the formal decision signed by Karadzic and the representatives of the Crisis Staff were ready to comply with Karadzic's order. The local representatives listened to me and they reorganised themselves as I directed." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although the situation that I found was one of quite a high level of autonomy of the Crisis Staffs, I must say that there was no opposition, at least not any public opposition, or in talking to me to the implementation of the decision on the establishment of commissions. However, obviously they had done everything before that in respect of the decision on the establishment of War Presidencies which had been published in the Official Gazette, namely, not to implement that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, on what day was the decision in relation to War Presidencies published in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision published in the gazette was the decision on the establishment of War Presidency which was not respected by the Crisis Staffs. And Mr. Karadzic was saying in that regard that he didn't have good communication with the field. As regards the decision on War Commissions, that differed because a physical person from Pale would go to the field and constitute an organ which would then be endorsed by the parliament. I didn't have time for -- to wait for that decision to be published in the Official Gazette, so I took the original of that decision on my tour of the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, what was your opinion of the decision of the Presidency to establish War Presidencies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that this was just window dressing, that nothing substantially changed, just the label of the Crisis Staff would be removed, the designation from the door; it would no longer stay Crisis Staff but War Presidency. And this is probably how it was perceived by people in the terrain, and they really were not inclined to change the title of their firm which was indicated on the door. I wanted to do something essential, something substantial to form at the municipal level an organ which would be directly entrusted by the republican Presidency with the establishment of these organs at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were asked about the level of autonomy of the Crisis Staffs, and you were specifically asked about what you heard when you went to the Presidency in relation to the communications between the Crisis Staffs and the Presidency that preceded your arrival in Pale on the 10th of June, 1992. I'd like to show you three documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Those documents are the following, Your Honour, two of them are Exhibit 529, one of them is tab 158, and the other is tab 193. The other document is Exhibit P54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the English version be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We do have copies for the Judges, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document that I wish to refer you to first is currently being distributed. Yes. The second document I'll refer to is the 6 May document, and the third one is the 5 June document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document that I wish to refer to first is the document from Exhibit 529, tab 193. Your Honours, I take it you have a copy of that document? It's the National Security Council minutes dated 28 April, 1992. I have copies here if you do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the only one we have not in front of us. You have distributed a lot of documents but not this one, as far as I can see. It certainly is preferred that you first distribute the documents you deal with first and then ... Now, we have in front of us the 28th of April, 1992, minutes of the meeting of the National Security Council and the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If the witness could have that document placed before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, if I could refer you to the heading on the document before you, and can you confirm that that's the minutes of the meeting of the National Security Council and the government of the Serb Republic of BH held on 28 April, 1992. And can I then refer you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, may I ask you, do you expect the witness to say that these are the minutes, has he been present during that meeting or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, he hasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now you ask the witness whether these are the minutes of which I just said it was. That's what the document says. There's no need to put this kind of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, can you please turn to the last page of the document before you. Could you read there that it is signed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just wondering if I could have a copy of the document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, you are entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, did Radovan Karadzic ever show you any copies of any of the minutes of the National Security Council?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I saw this document for the first time talking to the investigators of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, you refer you to paragraph 9 of that document and I note that it says that: "Reports were adopted on the work of Crisis Staff and municipal authorities." Did Radovan Karadzic ever tell you that any reports were received from -- on the work of Crisis Staffs in the National Security Council?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never spoke about that subject. It was only what I found out when I came to Pale and that at the previous Assembly, and Mr. Karadzic said they had discussed problems of communications, but we never discussed the National Security Council problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Djokanovic. If I could refer to the next document which is a document dated 6 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If that document could be placed before Dr. Djokanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P54, tab 529, which I think is also Exhibit 529, tab 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, in the opening paragraph of this document, it says that: "On the basis of the decision of the National Security Council of the Serbian Republic of BH, certain decisions have been taken." Did Radovan Karadzic ever tell you, or did anyone else ever tell you, that the Bratunac Crisis Staff took decisions implementing decisions of the National Security Council?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, I refer you to the next document, which is a document dated 5 June, 1992, marked to the attention of the President of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the authors of which are the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff. And this is Exhibit number 529, tab 158, and the heading on that document is "Report on activities." Did Radovan Karadzic or anyone else tell you that the Presidency received a report from the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff only days before you arrival in Pale?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Having seen those three documents, Dr. Djokanovic, do you consider that Radovan Karadzic informed you fully in relation to communications with Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are just two points that can be important. Novo Sarajevo has direct territorial communication with Pale and representatives from the Crisis Staff in Novo Sarajevo could physically reach Pale. And this does not apply to those from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, can you just tell me whether or not, having seen those documents, and having told the Court what you have in relation to your prior knowledge of them, do you now consider that Radovan Karadzic fully informed you in relation to communications with Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I look at these documents, then it is quite correct to say that he didn't inform me fully before I went out into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dr. Djokanovic, I'd like to move to another matter, and I'd like to refer you again to your statement, and that is your second statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours have a copy of the second statement there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It's at page 13, and it's the third last paragraph. And for Dr. Djokanovic, it's at page 14 in the B/C/S, and it's the third paragraph from the bottom. Again, Dr. Djokanovic doesn't have that statement so I will proceed to read it into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The paragraph reads as follows, Dr. Djokanovic: "The Presidency was the supreme commander over the military and the police. When I arrived in Pale from what I observed, I understood that there were contacts between the Presidency and the Main Staff every day in respect of various questions." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to present Dr. Djokanovic with one further document and that is Exhibit P65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps first ask the witness the following: You said this was your impression and your statement says: "From what I observed, I understood that there were contacts between the Presidency and the Main Staff every day." What observations make you understand that such daily contacts existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the building of the Presidency, we were together all day from morning till night, and it was simply impossible in those days not to discuss questions such as, Where is Mladic? Where is the generals from the Main Staff as they were in Han Pijesak and we were in Pale. So there was no problems in terms of physical communication. It was possible to communicate. And also there were telephone lines that were functioning. So that was my impression. But I can't remember a particular detail to be able to tell you I know that they spoke on that particular day, but my impression was that they did communicate daily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have telephone lines with the whole of the world, that doesn't mean that I call all of them. I mean, you say there was daily communication on the basis of your observations. Could you be a bit more precise? Would you see people walking into rooms or did you hear people making telephone calls? I mean, I'm seeking facts because you said, "On the basis of my observations, I understood ..." So I'd like to know what those observations were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that period of time, I was present on a number of occasions when Dr. Karadzic spoke on the phone with Mr. Mladic. I spoke with Mr. Mladic several times on the phone. So if members of the Presidency went to attend peace negotiations, then I would be left alone in the Presidency and I would answer the phone when the people from the Main Staff called up. So I spoke to General Mladic on a number of occasions. On one occasion, General Mladic and his associates came to the Presidency, so I'm afraid I couldn't say more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you have told us that you attended telephone conversations, that sometimes even people came, that you were involved in these communications yourself. The next question is you said it was every day. What observation supports that understanding? If I didn't have such an impression, I would have said, "I don't think it was on a daily basis," but I'm not able to provide evidence that it was on a daily basis but it was my impression. 10 or 15 days after my testimony, I would say that I had been in court every day even though Wednesday was a free day, but the impression I would have would be that I had been in the courtroom every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your testimony correctly if you say that on the basis of the frequency of these observations, you were left with the impression that it was if not every day, then at least at such a regular basis and such a frequent basis that that led you to understand it to be on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like now to present the witness with the document, Exhibit P65, tab 217 and we do have copies here for the Court and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This document is a declaration of the ending of the war, and it's dated 17 December 1992 and it's signed by Momcilo Krajisnik. Dr. Djokanovic, were you present at an Assembly session on the 17th of December, 1992, when this decision was reached?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the Assembly meeting in Zvornik, and I think we are, then I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you recall this decision being made?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Margetts. Is there any question arising from re-examination, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there's a fair chance that the questions by the Bench could not be answered within the -- yes, Mr. Krajisnik. Ms. Loukas, Mr. Krajisnik asks our attention. I don't know what he wants, I don't know whether you are aware -- of course you have an opportunity to consult with him, if you would like, having an interpreter ready.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask in line with the request I have addressed to you at the beginning of this testimony to be allowed to show certain things to this witness. I think it will be very useful. I think there is some misunderstanding here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, as I said, in exceptional circumstances, we would allow it but always after consultation with counsel. So if you would consult with counsel at this very moment, or if I would hear from counsel that there's no objection, then -- and then I would not allow you to just show matters to a witness but to put questions and, if necessary, for those questions to show something to the witness, you would be allowed to do so. But at first, you are to consult with counsel whether this is a matter that could not be dealt by counsel. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I only stand, Your Honour, because I think exceptional circumstances is what is required, and I haven't seen any exception circumstances offered at this point. Second of all, Mr. Krajisnik has two able counsel at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we have given a ruling that not under all circumstances we would exclude it, and if I would say no right away then of course that would not be fair in view of that ruling. So Mr. Krajisnik, you are first of all invited to consult with counsel. Perhaps it's even better to see whether that could be done during the break and then I'll hear from counsel and from you whether there's any need for any further questions and to confront the witness with any further documents. We will adjourn until 20 minutes to 1.00. I would like to add to that, Mr. Krajisnik, that of course your questions do not add to the time available for cross-examination, and since until now it's by far more the 60 per cent rule, the time that has been taken, it's not some additional time granted to the Defence. Please discuss it with counsel, we adjourn until 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just ask before Your Honours go. Could I just ask for a question of management and time table when Your Honours were proposing to deal with the particular issue which was mentioned earlier in relation to protective measures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we could deal with it now, but Mr. Gaynor is now not present anymore. So then I suggest that we do that immediately --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a couple of -- with respect, I apologise for interrupting, Your Honour, but I am trying to be helpful here. I have a couple of other practical matters which I could deal with while Mr. Gaynor is finding his way here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These practical matters are of such urgency that they are more important than to finish the testimony of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Very important to deal with today, Your Honour. I was just saying if Mr. Gaynor is finding his way through the building, I could helpfully use the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's be very practical. The witness may leave the courtroom. After the break, Mr. Djokanovic, you will be invited to answer some further questions. And, Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just this: That the witness timetable for the coming week has changed quite significantly, and I do understand that the Prosecution of course have considerable difficulties sometimes in obtaining the witnesses they want on the date they want them. The basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a matter which requires discussion in open court because otherwise it would be available to the parties immediately after the session at the very moment we stop. I'm available to further discussion practicalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, these matters should be discussed in open court. They -- they -- they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's this: The basic switch has been that there were originally going to be three witnesses in relation to one particular municipality, Ilijas. For various reasons that's become impossible, and in the last few days it's got switched around, and of course I understand Mr. Harmon is doing his best, I'm not quarrelling with that. We've ended up with -- programmed for next week two witnesses from Ilijas, one from Kljuc and one from Prijedor. The ones from Kljuc and Prijedor being 92 bis witnesses coming for cross-examination. Your Honour, that's more than a superficial change because the way that we divide up the work between ourselves on our side, and Your Honour in another decision commented that the Trial Chamber doesn't wish to become too much involved in time management issues as within the Defence team, is that I am doing all these witnesses next week, and Your Honour it is simply not practical for us on this side to unscramble that time management issue. So I am doing next weeks' witnesses. Dealing with two witnesses from Ilijas, another witness from Kljuc, where there have been several witnesses who have already given evidence, and then the first witness we've had in this case from Prijedor, is a totally different picture from dealing with three witnesses from a single municipality. And just to mention, without going into too much detail, Your Honour, the Prijedor witness, 92 bis, there is absolutely hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of pages of previous transcript. He's given evidence on -- I think it's four, I would be corrected if it's three, but I believe it's four previous occasions. Your Honour, the reason I mention it now is this: That I'm in a quandary. If I say to Your Honours today that there is a severe risk, or if I were to say I would not be able to deal with all these witnesses in the course of next week, then based on past experience Your Honours would say to me, well, it's only Friday and you've got several days, do your best, and we expect you to be ready. If I leave it until next week then, Your Honours will say to me and the Prosecution will say, well, this witness is already here, he's come all the way from Bosnia, we must deal with him, he can't go back. So I'm conscientiously putting the risk before the Trial Chamber now, Your Honour, because I am saying that there is a severe risk that I will at some point next week have to say to Your Honours, No, this is simply too much, we have not been able to deal with it. We cannot be able to proceed with all these witnesses but ... Your Honour, that's all I'm saying right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then about -- then we should turn into protective measures for KRAJ 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I specifically indicated earlier when this first came up that there was a certain element that I wish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. You wanted to do it in open. I'd forgotten that. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I also say -- just to take 10 seconds on timing, Your Honour. Would Your Honours respectfully please remember that this is our response, this is not an oral supplement of another response. This is our response to the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, my first question with respect for the Bench is whether the Trial Chamber has had the opportunity, or has taken the opportunity which is the key point, to look at the UNHCR report which was cited in the Prosecution motion in relation to this and other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that we had the whole of the report presented; is that correct, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just the quotations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct. I have a copy here if Your Honours wish me to submit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please provide it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, what the -- what the Prosecution did was they very helpfully gave the -- the -- into that -- web reference -- the -- in the footnote, so it was -- it was possible to track it down that way. But anyway, Your Honours now have it. Your Honour, I wanted particularly just to draw attention to a couple of items in that report in relation to the citations and the motion. If we look at paragraph 6, and of course we're talking about the public elements of this motion right now, if we look at paragraph 6 of the motion, "special attention" is where that passage starts and Your Honours find that at page 2 of the -- the main report. But there, Your Honour, I simply wish to remark that the incidents on the fifth line, for example, in 2002, ICT [sic] witnesses were on at least two occasions the target of violence. I'm not minimising it Your Honour, if I simply point out that that was three years ago. Those are the specific examples adopted. And the further example given in May 2004, the brother of a war crime suspect, et cetera, et cetera, two points there. One is the -- that is put in terms of it is being argued that the informer was targeted in order to silence him. So that's the highest it's put there. But secondly, this is plainly from the nature of the description, what you might call a high-level matter, relating specifically to Dr. Karadzic and relating to an informant. It's an utterly different category. So far as this -- without in any way disparaging the fine work in these reports of the UNHCR, when it comes to that sort of matter it is this Trial Chamber and the experience of this Tribunal which is much more pertinent than that sort of report from a body which, with much wider and different responsibilities. So far as paragraph 7 of the motion is concerned, it is worth looking at introductory sentence before the passage cited because in the report at 2.2 on page 3, we find four lines into that paragraph the sentence beginning "However, as evidenced" and that's where the citation and the motion picks up. And what has been significantly omitted from the citation is the preceding sentence, "in most return locations, the security situation has steadily improved and many returning communities report that relations with local residents are good and that the local police are acting professionally." And that's a pretty significant sentence to have omitted, be -- given that the basis of this public -- of the motion is to draw the Court's attention to continuing security difficulties in Bosnia. Coupled with that observation, a phrase about four or five lines into the cited passage is "serious incidents continue to occur in certain areas." Now again, the UNHCR report is dealing with that in reasonably general terms. It's the obligation, we submit, of the party who is applying for protective measures, in this case, to be more specific in relation to such matters and to indicate whether, indeed, this area is one of those areas. The -- so far as the citation in paragraph 9 is concerned -- I only skip over paragraph 8 because I don't want to take time on something there which is not specifically -- the citation in paragraph 8 is nothing specifically to do with evidence before a Tribunal, evidence certainly before this Tribunal, it's a general -- a remark in relation to some violent incidents, and such incidents are not unknown in many, many countries in Europe, let alone parts of the world. Paragraph 9, the citation there, the introductory sentence there, it's at page 8 of the report itself, the introductory sentence makes it quite clear that it's dealing with a particular question of relocation or what is called internal flight or relocation alternative. It's the first large paragraph on page 8 of the report. "The victims of war crimes or for witnesses testifying before local courts or the ICTY, the concept of an internal flight or relocation alternative should not in UNHCR's view be considered relevant." They're dealing with, in essence, the fact that in a small relatively small country like Bosnia and Herzegovina, just moving somebody to some other part of the country doesn't reliably solve the problem, if there is a problem in the first place. But it doesn't tell you whether there's a problem in the first place. I would also comment that in its reference there in the cited passage where it talks about, "Because of the number of indicted war criminals still at large, insufficiencies of the rule of law system generally and in view of the absence of effective witness protection in particular, a victim or witness of war crimes who is being returned to BiH would be exposed to serious risk of safety even in the" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will slow down. "A victim or witness of war crimes who is being returned to BiH would be exposed to serious risk of safety even in the area of relocation." That is, for the purposes of this Trial Chamber, with respect -- which is not the purpose for which this report is written, of course, that is far too broadly stated. It cannot be universally true. It's also not easy to see why a victim who is not a witness or prospective witness is at this point then especially exposed. So those are some remarks in relation to the report which is put forward as, if you like, a general foundation for this specific application. We'd also like, before I then move very quickly into the area where it would be appropriate to go into private session, to just stress what the Defence does strongly urge is the correct approach which is incumbent upon the party seeking protective measures to give as far as possible the whole picture to the Tribunal and not to -- to the Trial Chamber and not to give a selective picture which then puts the onus on the other party of coming back and saying, Well, that's not right. This should not be treated, applications for protective measures, as a simple adversarial process. It is the duty of all concerned in this matter - Prosecution, Defence, and of course the Trial Chamber - to ensure that the cutting down of the public nature of the trial is confined in the absolute minimum so with those prefacing remarks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, also have the French side, I receive a message whether you'd slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will. I apologise for that. I'm always anxious not to take any more time than necessary, but I realise that going too fast doesn't help anybody. So I'm slowing down, Your Honour, and I'm slowing down as I then indicate that this is the point at which it would be appropriate, in my submission, to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn it to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The application just made in the absence of the witness needs some more attention, so therefore I ask the witness to leave the courtroom but remain standby. The issue of scheduling for next week and protective measures for Witness 60 will be considered the Bench immediately after this session. That means that you'll know even if the decision have not issued in open court yet, and even if it would be an oral decision that you will at least be aware of what the consequences of our decision will be. Then the Chamber first wants to finish the examination of this witness. But one pending question was whether Mr. Krajisnik had any additional questions. I also understood that he wanted to confront the witness with certain documents. Mr. Stewart, you have been consulted by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, certainly. Thank you for the opportunity. Yes, Your Honour, the position is this: May I say straight away because this is once again a situation where I am in public and open conflict and difference with my client, and I apologise to him and he understands that manfully and we've agreed to differ in a sense. But here we are differing, Your Honour, it's most unfortunate. But I applied, in my submissions to Your Honour here, this criterion: If Ms. Loukas, having finished the cross-examination, had then -- we'd had a break and she had come to me, as she often would and I to her as well, of course, to get her views on these things. If she had come to me and said, Well, how about exploring these other areas? If cross-examination had been not quite finished and we were in a break, and she said, Shall we explore these other areas and how about putting these further documents. And she had suggested to me doing exactly what it is that Mr. Krajisnik is now proposing that should be done and explored, I would have said to Ms. Loukas, I would have said, No, this is one of those occasions where we leave it where it is. And that's our judgment and that's the way we run the case. I wouldn't in fact expect any disagreement to arise between Ms. Loukas and me as it generally doesn't between two experienced counsel in relation to these matters. So that's my criterion, Your Honour. And on that criterion, I have the conduct of the case with Ms. Loukas's able assistance, and it's not in a situation, with respect, which we believe that the conduct of the case should be rested away from us in that way, despite these strong and in many ways understandable anxious concerns of a defendant who is on trial for such serious charges. We understand those concerns of our client extremely well, we hope, Your Honour, but we don't agree with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, is there anything you'd like to add to what Mr. Stewart said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would not like it to be seen that I am dissatisfied with the way my counsel are working. I believe Ms. Loukas did an excellent job and I think that today, she was perhaps sidetracked, and please let the Prosecution bear with me, when she was cut short on a number of occasions by the Prosecution. She has failed to cover some important areas, therefore. I assure you that this witness is quite certain of what he is saying, but he is also proceeding under a misconception. So in order to ascertain the truth, which I believe we all believe is important, it will be beneficial to all. That is why I am suggesting this. We fail to see whether someone actually took any action after his reporting on any crimes, so we need to assess whether everything that could have been done at a certain point in the past could have -- was done. Then we want to see whether Mr. Krajisnik was indeed a member of the Presidency at that point or wasn't because basically everything which is in the Prosecution's case is something which is reflected in the statement of this witness, and I appreciate that, but the whole job has not been finished properly today. And I believe that you, Your Honours, could also see that for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an appalling situation. If we take the hypothesis that I put forward where Ms. Loukas and I were having a discussion and we decided not to proceed with cross-examination, we would then not come into the Trial Chamber and lay before the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution those areas which we had decided not to explore. The position that the Trial Chamber has put us in with this ruling that even in exceptional circumstances is creating constant conflict and constant difficulty, and we do urge Your Honours to retract this destructive ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invited Mr. Krajisnik because he had requested to put questions and since he had consulted, I wanted actually to know whether he persisted to do that. I do understand that you are not happy with the situation. We'll consider whether the ruling should change. But, Mr. Krajisnik, let me be quite clear on one issue. That is, that when we considered that, under certain circumstances, we would allow you to put some questions, that it was in the situation where your knowledge of the area would more -- be more practical for you to present these questions. But what now happens is a totally different situation, that is, the situation where it's not more practical that you perhaps add one or two questions in specific fields because of your special knowledge, but we are now in a situation where you seem to disagree with counsel on what's the best way to deal with certain aspects of the case. You've chosen to be represented by counsel, and especially in view of what you've said before, and apart from whatever opportunities you'll get, if it ever comes to that, to present your own case, that it's either of the two, apart from practical problems that could be easily overcome by one or two additional questions such as: Do you still remember the number plate of that car? Or would you know what the colour was of that building? Where of course if the witness says it's blue and you know it's a different colour, then it would be easier for you to put the next question, was the whole of the building white or blue? But this, we have now come to a situation where two Defence strategies in respect of this particular witness seem to emerge, and it's for you to resolve that with counsel, and we are in no way in a situation the Chamber has envisaged when it would not, under all circumstances, exclude you to put some additional questions to a witness. Therefore, your request is denied. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not a question of a change in strategy. For were it a question of a strange of strategy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, there is a ruling. That means we'll proceed with this witness and it's not -- I'll not give you an opportunity to reopen the debate on the matter we just ruled on. So therefore, we'll ask Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djokanovic, Judge Canivell has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Very briefly. When you returned from Zvornik to Pale and you communicated to the members of the leadership who were in Pale about what you learned in Zvornik, what was the reaction of the people to whom you communicated all this? What did you, yourself, Witness?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not approve of what had happened in Zvornik. It was agreed that I go there as soon as possible to take the documents on appointments of commissions, and those documents were signed on the 17th in the mornings. So I returned on the 16th in the afternoon, spoke to the Presidency, and by the 17th, these documents on the appointment of commissions were issued and then these documents were taken to those municipalities. I also spoke to Mr. Karadzic prior to the meeting all the commissioners in the mentioned municipalities, Dr. Karadzic, General Mladic and myself, and I said to Dr. Karadzic that he must pay close attention when talking to the people down there that all kinds of things had happened in the field. I don't believe that they are not aware of what had actually happened there - meaning the commissioners - and that this joint meeting will one day be of the greatest importance. Dr. Karadzic accepted all this. He took a Dictaphone to that meeting, and I remember well that he carefully chose his words as he spoke at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that what you saw at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were together. We were sitting next to one another, Dr. Karadzic, General Mladic and myself. Dr. Karadzic in the middle, Mladic on one side, and me on the other of Mr. Karadzic. We were the state delegation that went to talk to representatives of the mentioned municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether we are talking about the same. When you returned from Zvornik in mid-June, 1992, you reported to the persons who were there, the leaders, the leadership of Republika Srpska, among whom, of course, Mr. Krajisnik as well, and did you notice any particular reaction on their part to what you were telling them? You simply said that Mr. Krajisnik took a machine to record what you were saying, that's all.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was quite sure that the gentlemen in the Presidency fully shared my opinion and views about these matters in the field. Never for a moment did I notice anything else and that is why I had the energy to go back into the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting you. But that means if they shared their opinion, it means that they already knew what had happened. Maybe not in every detail, but they knew what had happened in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they were aware of the details. I think they had some news as to what was happening in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, it seems there may be some confusion there. At page 87, there's -- that's right, page 87, line 9, Dr. Karadzic accepted all, he took a Dictaphone to that meeting, referring to Dr. Karadzic. And then when you look at page 87, line 25, Your Honour is saying: You simply said that Mr. Krajisnik took a machine to record what you were saying. That's all. So there seems to be a reference to Mr. Karadzic having a Dictaphone and then a reference to Mr. Krajisnik having a Dictaphone, and there does seem to be some confusion there because the first reference is to Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you clarify that issue? You have heard what Ms. Loukas said about who exactly had the Dictaphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I noticed on the screen, it was Dr. Karadzic who had the Dictaphone. I was speaking about Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Hanoteau has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please look at your witness statement number 2, could it be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Hanoteau, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: Statement number 2, page 6, please. [Interpretation] Do you have page 6 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, in the third paragraph, it is stated, that: "The attitude of the deputies... [In English] ... to the abuses that occurred in the field meant that this issue was not raised as an agenda item at the republican Assembly." [Interpretation] Are you saying that the deputies had knowledge of what was happening in the field and that they preferred not to talk about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be almost unbelievable if they hadn't known. Most of those deputies were either members of Crisis Staffs later commissions, and they were doing their work as peoples's deputies. They were elected in 1990 when there were elections by constituencies, so it was exactly known where each deputy had come from, and it was his job to take care of the situation in his constituency where he had been elected. So when I was discussing the fact that I was not appointed to the government, that was the whole point, not whether I should be a minister or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is: In your opinion, did they make the deliberate choice not to speak about it publicly? They were aware of what was happening but they made the choice not to speak about it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite certain of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second point, please. Please look at page 8. In the one but last paragraph, you say, [In English] "The rest of the leadership did not react strongly enough to the war crimes. If at that time, 10 people that were involved in things would have been put on trial, things would have taken a different course." [Interpretation] I would like you to clarify this statement. Does this mean that at this particular point in time, the leaders, Karadzic and the other leaders, still could have informed the courts, undertaken arrests, and have those guilty of war crimes taken to justice. Was it possible to use the judicial apparatus to judge the culprits straight away to set an example which would have stopped further violence.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite certain that they did have the support of the people, had they taken such a step. Because in the plebescite, the people said that they wanted to live with the people of other ethnicities, and it was on that basis that we adopted the constitution which is explicit saying that all citizens are equal before the law. So they had the support of the people, they had the support of the constitution, but they chose to be opportunist, supporting a smaller radical group of politicians and probably a radical segment of the population as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You haven't quite answered my question. It had to do whether there was a judicial apparatus at that time that could have functioned and that could have been informed. Were there trials that could have taken these cases?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, there was the Prosecutor's office, there were courts, there was the Ministry of Justice. Now, in which stage of constitution municipal courts, district courts and the Prosecutor's office were, I don't know, but I do know that these existed. The courts, the police, the Ministry of Justice and the constitution which regulated all these matters as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another point, please, sir. During your testimony or rather the first statement, the other document that you have in front of you, [In English] statement number one, [Interpretation] You have the document in front of you, turn to page 11, please. Page 11 of the English version. The one but last paragraph, you said: [In English] "In June 1992, Karadzic and Krajisnik had the most authority in the War Presidency. I think Krajisnik controlled the majority of the deputies in the Serb Assembly. I considered that he had established a non-legal parliamentary party." [Interpretation] Could you comment on what you meant by "non-legal parliamentary party," please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large number of peoples' deputies at that point in time did not enjoy prestige in the municipality in which they lived. They were accused of various affairs such as arms struggling [as interpreted] and even arms smuggling and, as such, instead of leaving politics, they were awarded and they climbed up in the hierarchy. They became republican commissioners, they became professional deputies in the assemblies, and they became a part of a lobby which in its later political activities relied mostly on the President of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Another point. I'd like to be quite clear about your answer. You said a moment ago - and I think that was what I gathered from your whole testimony - that all the deputies in the Assembly were also members of Crisis Staffs. Is my understanding correct or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't have the precise data, but I said that most of the deputies in the People's Assembly were in their constituencies also members of Crisis Staffs and commissions. A large number of them were republican commissioners in the second half of 1992, they were responsible for constituting municipalities in a part of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And by whom were they designated? To be members of these Crisis Staffs they must have been appointed by someone.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they couldn't appoint themselves. This was a period when a part of the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, one of the ruling parties in the territory in which it is majority appoints a Crisis Staff. If we're talking about the Serb Republic, the ruling and only influential party at that time was the one that appointed Crisis Staffs. Of course they didn't have time to think about each individual member of the Crisis Staff. They didn't have the references for these people, so that there were many omissions and I don't think they were intentional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the War Commissions that came after the Crisis Staffs, were the same deputies members of these new institutions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with a decision on the formation of municipal commissions, they would be composed of a president of the leading municipal party, a deputy, a prestigious businessman and a prestigious figure, so when such commissions were formed, deputies had to be a member. Then some deputies were actually republican commissioners and were involved in these activities as well. After the municipal -- municipalities were established, I don't know whether they held positions in the executive powers. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last point: In these Crisis Staffs, first of all, and in the War Commissions as well, was there someone representing the army and the police or the army or the police, either the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I have explained the formula. The republican commissioner, the national deputy, president of the municipal board of the party, a prominent citizen and a prominent businessman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'm not sure on that last question. It seems that there's a reference to both Crisis Staffs and War Commissions. I'm not entirely certain that the witness's answer addresses both of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have understood the doubt expressed by Mr. Margetts whether your answer covers both Crisis Staffs and War Commissions or just War Commissions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was speaking about the formula regarding the commissions, I was explicit; I was talking about the War Commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then was there someone representing the army and police in the Crisis Staffs? Because that was the other part of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the commissions, no member of these institutions were there. I would know if in a municipality one of the brigade commanders or his assistants may have been nominated; no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. The question was whether there were such representatives in the Crisis Staffs, so that's in an earlier stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were certainly representatives of the police but not the army because the army had still not been constituted. Something close to the army would be secretariats for national defence, so someone from that secretariat would probably be a member of that Crisis Staff because that is a segment of the executive in the municipality. So someone from the secretariat for national defence and someone from the police would be in the Crisis Staff. Who in the hierarchy, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that answer. I've got a few questions for you as well. First of all, in one of your statements, you're referring to what I would call the Velibor Ostojic incident where he was removed from his car by paramilitaries, and then your statement reads, "Only after ..." "Ostojic told me about this incident and I think this was the drop that overfilled the cup and caused the Republika Srpska to intervene." Could you tell us, when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall with precision but we were deep into the second half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that means after the summer. Or could you be a bit more precise because "deep into the second half" could be Christmas but could be the end of August as well. Where would I have to ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there was reference to grass, there was no snow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is a logical answer and perhaps my reference to Christmas is also a bit unlucky one because Christmas is not at the same date everywhere. So you would say late summer, is that a ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From this incident, could we draw any conclusions in respect of the power to intervene the republican -- the Republika Srpska power to intervene and to end -- put an end to situations that were not welcome or can we not? I mean, to what extent is this an example or is just not an example of such power?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN DJOKANOVIC [Resumed]
